$$C(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k+1}}{(2k)!(4k+1)}, \qquad S(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+3}}{(2k+1)!(4k+3)}, \qquad \operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k+1}}{k!(2k+1)}, \qquad \operatorname{erfc}(z)=1-\operatorname{erf}(z).$$

The following local lemmas prove convergence and show that $C,S,\operatorname{erf}$
equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

For $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$ with $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ and $|z|<1$,
define

$$(a)_0=1,\qquad (a)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(a+j),\qquad {}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}z^k.$$

Only this Gauss-series branch of ${}_2F_1$ is defined on this page; no value
outside $|z|<1$ or across a continuation cut is implicit.

derivations.claim: For a nonzero term, the Pochhammer product gives $h_{k+1}/h_k=z(a+k)(b+k)/((c+k)(k+1))$. For $k\ge N>|c|$, $|a+k|\le k(1+|a|/N)$, $|b+k|\le k(1+|b|/N)$, $|c+k|\ge k(1-|c|/N)$, and $k+1\ge k$. These inequalities yield the stated $q_N$.

As $N\to\infty$, $q_N\to|z|<1$, so a finite $N$ has $q_N<1$; summing the geometric majorant proves the tail bound and local uniform convergence on compact subsets of $|z|<1$. If $a$ or $b$ is a nonpositive integer, its Pochhammer product becomes zero after finitely many terms, which proves the terminating case.

For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

derivations.claim: For either term sequence, cancellation of the factorials gives $|a_{k+1}|/|a_k|=|z|^2/[4(k+1)(k+n+1)]$ whenever $a_k\ne0$; at $z=0$ the series are finite-valued directly. This ratio decreases to $0$.

For $k\ge K+1$ the ratios are at most $q$, so $\sum_{k=K+1}^{\infty}|a_k|\le |a_{K+1}|\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^j =|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$. On every disk $|z|\le R$, the ratio is bounded by the same expression with $R$ in place of $|z|$, which is eventually below $1$; the Weierstrass test gives uniform convergence there.

A derivative of order $d\in\{1,2\}$ multiplies the $k$th monomial by a factor bounded by $(2k+n)^d$ and lowers its power by $d$. The ratio of successive absolute differentiated terms is therefore $r_k$ times a factor that tends to $1$; on each disk it is eventually bounded by a constant below $1$. Thus both differentiated series converge uniformly on compact disks and may be differentiated termwise.

For every complex number $z$,

$$\frac1{\Gamma(z)}=ze^{\gamma z}\prod_{n\ge1}\left(1+\frac{z}{n}\right)e^{-z/n}.$$

with locally uniform convergence on $\mathbb C$.

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let each $f_n:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$. Then $f$ is holomorphic and

$$f_n^{(k)}\longrightarrow f^{(k)}$$

locally uniformly on $\Omega$ for every natural $k$, with $f^{(0)}=f$.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$ the $k$th derivatives converge locally uniformly to the $k$th derivative of the limit.

derivations.claim: For $w=z/n$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, the path $1+tw$ lies in the principal-logarithm domain. Its derivative integrand is continuous on $[0,1]$ and is integrable by [F4]. By [F2], [F3], and the chain rule, $$\operatorname{Log}(1+w)=\int_0^1\frac{w}{1+tw}\,dt, \qquad w-\operatorname{Log}(1+w)=\int_0^1\frac{tw^2}{1+tw}\,dt.$$ Since $|1+tw|^2=1+2t\operatorname{Re}w+t^2|w|^2\ge1$, the summand has absolute value at most $|z|^2/(2n^2)$. Summing this bound is uniform on every compact subset of the right half-plane. Each summand is holomorphic there, so the series converges locally uniformly and defines a holomorphic function by [F5].

For each finite $N$, exponentiating the partial sum gives $$\exp\left(-\operatorname{Log}z-\gamma_Ez+ \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(\frac zn-\operatorname{Log}(1+z/n)\right)\right) =\left(ze^{\gamma_Ez}\prod_{n=1}^{N}(1+z/n)e^{-z/n}\right)^{-1}.$$ Taking $N\to\infty$, local uniform convergence from step 1.1 and [F1] show that the left side tends to $e^{\ell_+(z)}$ and the right side to $\Gamma(z)$. This proves the claimed branch identity.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For any finite complex rectangle on which the principal branch is defined,
every finite output for a requested complex node of
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for $\exp$ or
$\operatorname{Log}$ contains the exact image. For the same typed DAG and
designated complex output node, nested input rectangles on the same admissible
branch, fixed constant enclosures, and the same finite dyadic format and
truncation index give nested finite enclosures whenever both calls return
finite results. Rectangles meeting zero, the negative real
branch cut, or an unresolved quadrant return the declared domain or
inconclusive status.

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

The following local lemmas prove convergence and show that $C,S,\operatorname{erf}$
equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

For $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$ with $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ and $|z|<1$,
define

$$(a)_0=1,\qquad (a)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(a+j),\qquad {}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}z^k.$$

Only this Gauss-series branch of ${}_2F_1$ is defined on this page; no value
outside $|z|<1$ or across a continuation cut is implicit.

For the terms $c_k$ of $C$ and $s_k$ of $S$ in
[[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]],

$$\frac{|c_{k+1}|}{|c_k|}\le \frac{\pi^2|z|^4/4}{(2k+1)(2k+2)}, \qquad \frac{|s_{k+1}|}{|s_k|}\le \frac{\pi^2|z|^4/4}{(2k+2)(2k+3)}.$$

Once the applicable bound is at most $q<1$ for all terms after a first
omitted term, the absolute tail is bounded by that term divided by $1-q$.
Both series converge locally uniformly on $\mathbb C$ and equal the integrals
of $\cos(\pi t^2/2)$ and $\sin(\pi t^2/2)$ from $0$ to $z$.

For the $k$th term $e_k$ of the $\operatorname{erf}$ series in
[[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]],

$$\frac{|e_{k+1}|}{|e_k|} =\frac{|z|^2}{k+1}\frac{2k+1}{2k+3} \le\frac{|z|^2}{k+1}.$$

Thus, if $|z|^2/(K+2)=q<1$, the tail after terms $0,\ldots,K$ is bounded by
$|e_{K+1}|/(1-q)$. The series converges locally uniformly and equals
$2/\sqrt\pi$ times the integral of $e^{-t^2}$ from $0$ to $z$.

Let $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$, $|z|<1$, and
$c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$. For the nonterminating Gauss-series term
$h_k=(a)_k(b)_kz^k/((c)_kk!)$, and any integer $N>|c|$,

$$\frac{|h_{k+1}|}{|h_k|} =|z|\frac{|a+k||b+k|}{|c+k|(k+1)} \le q_N:=|z|\frac{(1+|a|/N)(1+|b|/N)}{1-|c|/N} \qquad(k\ge N).$$

For sufficiently large $N$, $q_N<1$; then the tail starting at $h_N$ is at
most $|h_N|/(1-q_N)$. If $a$ or $b$ is a nonpositive integer, the series
terminates and its tail after the last nonzero term is zero.

The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],

\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$

$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$

$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

If a Gauss series terminates because $a$ or $b$ is a nonpositive integer, the procedure forms its finite sum using the backend and skips the infinite-tail stage.

Otherwise, at each permitted term count $N$, it encloses the partial sum through index $N-1$ using [A1]. When it passes, adding the symmetric interval enlargement by the resulting tail bound contains the full series value by [F2]--[F5].

The procedure returns `success` only when the resulting enclosure passes the radius test in [F1] and any reported relative test also passes; it returns `range` if the backend reports a representational failure. If no iteration within the finite caps passes, it returns `inconclusive`. The preceding inclusion proof applies to every successful enclosure, while the bounded loops and explicit failure branches ensure that the procedure terminates.

For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

For $n\ge0$ and either series in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]], the
absolute term ratio is

$$r_k=\frac{|z|^2}{4(k+1)(k+n+1)}.$$

The series for $J_n$ and $I_n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly in
$z\in\mathbb C$. If $K\ge0$ and
$q=|z|^2/[4(K+2)(K+n+2)]<1$, then the tail after terms $k=0,\ldots,K$ has
absolute value at most $|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$, where $a_k$ is the corresponding
series term. The first two differentiated series also converge locally
uniformly.

derivations.claim: Multiplying the two exponential series gives, uniformly for $|t|=1$, $$e^{(z/2)(t-t^{-1})} =\left(\sum_{p\ge0}\frac{(z/2)^pt^p}{p!}\right) \left(\sum_{q\ge0}\frac{(-z/2)^qt^{-q}}{q!}\right).$$ The coefficient of $t^n$ for $n\ge0$ is $\sum_{q\ge0}(-1)^q(z/2)^{2q+n}/((q+n)!q!)=J_n(z)$.

Similarly, the coefficient of $t^n$ in $e^{(z/2)(t+t^{-1})}$ is $\sum_{q\ge0}(z/2)^{2q+n}/((q+n)!q!)=I_n(z)$. Coefficients are recovered by integrating the uniformly absolutely convergent Laurent series against $e^{-in\theta}$ on $t=e^{i\theta}$.

With $z=x\in\mathbb R$ and $t=e^{i\theta}$, the first generating function is $e^{ix\sin\theta}$; pairing $\theta$ and $-\theta$ gives the real cosine integral for $J_n$. The second is $e^{x\cos\theta}$; its sine Fourier component vanishes by symmetry, giving the displayed $I_n$ integral.
For $x\ge0$, every term in the series for $I_n(x)$ is nonnegative, so $I_n(x)\ge0$. The integral gives $e^{-x}I_n(x)\le\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi e^{-x(1-\cos\theta)}d\theta\le1$, since $1-\cos\theta\ge0$.

On $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\ell_+(z)=-\operatorname{Log}z-\gamma_Ez+ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac zn-\operatorname{Log}\left(1+\frac zn\right)\right).$$

Here $\operatorname{Log}$ is the principal logarithm from
[[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]], and
$\gamma_E$ denotes Euler's constant $\gamma$ from
[[def-euler-mascheroni-constant]]. Both $z$ and $1+z/n$ lie in the
principal-logarithm domain. The local uniform convergence of this series
and the identity $e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$ are established by
[[lem-loggamma-series-convergence-and-gamma-identity]].

For every $z$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, the series defining
$\ell_+(z)$ in [[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]] converges locally
uniformly, defines a holomorphic function, and satisfies
$e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$ for Euler's Gamma function on that half-plane.

The **Euler-Mascheroni constant** is

$$ \gamma:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1n-\log N\right), $$

provided the limit exists.

For $n\ge1$, let

$$H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1k,\qquad \gamma_n=H_n-\log n.$$

The sequence $(\gamma_n)$ is strictly decreasing and is bounded below by
$1-\log2$. It therefore converges to a constant $\gamma$ satisfying
$0<\gamma<1$, and

$$H_n=\log n+\gamma+o(1).$$

Consequently, $H_n/\log n\to1$ as $n\to\infty$, with the quotient considered
for $n\ge2$.

$n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n$ as the positive integer $n$ tends to infinity.

Equivalently,

$$\frac{n!}{\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n}\longrightarrow1\qquad(n\to\infty,\ n\ge1).$$

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $E \subseteq [a,b]$ be finite
([[def-countable]], [[def-equinumerous]]), and let $g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$
satisfy

$$g(x) \;=\; f(x) \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b] \setminus E .$$

Then $g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and

$$\int_a^b g \;=\; \int_a^b f .$$

In particular the values of an integrand at the endpoints of the interval, and at
any finite set of points, are irrelevant to both questions.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

On $[n,n+1]$, $\Phi'=f$ and [F7] gives $$\int_n^{n+1}\frac{f(u)}{u+z}\,du =\left[\frac{\Phi(u)}{u+z}\right]_{n}^{n+1} +\int_n^{n+1}\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du =\int_n^{n+1}\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du,$$ since $\Phi(n)=\Phi(n+1)=0$. On each $[n,n+1]$, write $f(u)=n+\tfrac12-u=(n+z+\tfrac12)-(u+z)$. By [F5] the function $(n+z+\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(u+z)-u$ has derivative $f(u)/(u+z)$; its derivative is continuous and integrable on the compact interval by [F6]. Applying [F6] and summing the resulting endpoint differences yields $$I_N(z)=(N+z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(N+z) -(z+\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}z-N-\log((N-1)!) -zH_{N-1}+\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\left(\frac zk-\operatorname{Log}(1+z/k)\right).$$ The coefficient of each internal $\operatorname{Log}(k+z)$ in the endpoint sum is $-1$. For $k\ge1$, $\operatorname{Log}(k+z)=\log k+\operatorname{Log}(1+z/k)$ because $k>0$ is real and multiplication by it preserves the principal argument; [F9] gives $\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\log k=\log((N-1)!)$. Add $-\operatorname{Log}z-\gamma_Ez$ to the finite sum in step 2.2. By [F1]--[F3], the resulting left side converges to $\ell_+(z)$, while $$\ell_+(z)=I_N(z)-(N+z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(N+z) +(z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}z+N+\log((N-1)!) +z(H_{N-1}-\gamma_E)+o(1).$$

Taking logarithms in [F4] is valid by continuity [F8]. The laws [F9] and $e=\exp(1)$ give $$\log(n!)=(n+\tfrac12)\log n-n+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)+o(1).$$ At $n=N-1$, since $\log(1-1/N)=-1/N+O(N^{-2})$, this becomes $$\log((N-1)!)=(N-\tfrac12)\log N-N+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)+o(1).$$ The logarithm estimate follows by integrating $1/(1-t)$ on $[0,1/N]$; the difference from $1/N$ is bounded by $1/(N^2(1-1/N))$. Also [F3] gives $H_{N-1}-\gamma_E=\log N+o(1)$. Therefore $(N+z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(N+z) =(N+z-\tfrac12)\log N+z+o(1)$.

Substitute these asymptotics into step 3.1. For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

For $n\ge0$ and either series in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]], the
absolute term ratio is

$$r_k=\frac{|z|^2}{4(k+1)(k+n+1)}.$$

The series for $J_n$ and $I_n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly in
$z\in\mathbb C$. If $K\ge0$ and
$q=|z|^2/[4(K+2)(K+n+2)]<1$, then the tail after terms $k=0,\ldots,K$ has
absolute value at most $|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$, where $a_k$ is the corresponding
series term. The first two differentiated series also converge locally
uniformly.

derivations.claim: By [F2] we may differentiate termwise. For a monomial $z^{2k+n}$, $(z^2D^2+zD-n^2)z^{2k+n}=4k(k+n)z^{2k+n}$. The coefficient ratio in [F1] is $a_k/a_{k-1}=\mp1/[4k(k+n)]$ for $k\ge1$, with the minus sign for $J_n$ and plus sign for $I_n$. Thus the coefficient of each power cancels in the respective differential equation.

For $J_{n-1}+J_{n+1}$, reindex the $J_{n+1}$ series so both terms have power $z^{2k+n-1}$. For $k\ge1$ their combined coefficient is $(-1)^kn/[2^{2k+n-1}k!(k+n)!]$, and for $k=0$ it is $1/[2^{n-1}(n-1)!]$. These are exactly the coefficients of $(2n/z)J_n$. For $I_{n-1}-I_{n+1}$ the same reindexing gives the same positive combined coefficient, proving the second recurrence.
Differentiating the $J_0$ series termwise and reindexing $k=j+1$ gives $$J_0'(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{j+1}z^{2j+1}}{2^{2j+1}j!(j+1)!} =-J_1(z).$$
Setting $z=0$ in the convergent series leaves only the $k=0,n=0$ term; every term has a positive power of $z$ when $n\ge1$. Hence the stated limits hold.

On $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\ell_+(z)=-\operatorname{Log}z-\gamma_Ez+ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac zn-\operatorname{Log}\left(1+\frac zn\right)\right).$$

Here $\operatorname{Log}$ is the principal logarithm from
[[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]], and
$\gamma_E$ denotes Euler's constant $\gamma$ from
[[def-euler-mascheroni-constant]]. Both $z$ and $1+z/n$ lie in the
principal-logarithm domain. The local uniform convergence of this series
and the identity $e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$ are established by
[[lem-loggamma-series-convergence-and-gamma-identity]].

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or

from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any

domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or

$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its

dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or

For the product branch, let $R_W$ be an outward upper bound for $\sup_{w\in W}|w|$ and try permitted integers $N$ until $N>2R_W$ or the finite cap is reached. For the Stirling branch, put $a_W=\inf\operatorname{Re}W>0$. Every $w\in W$ lies in the closed sector $|\arg w|\le\pi/2$, and $|w|\ge a_W$. By [F6] with $\delta=\pi/2$, its remainder has modulus at most $1/(4a_W)$. The procedure encloses the main term over $W$ using [A1], enlarges by this common radius, and subtracts the same shift-log enclosures from [F4]. For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

For $n\ge0$ and either series in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]], the
absolute term ratio is

$$r_k=\frac{|z|^2}{4(k+1)(k+n+1)}.$$

The series for $J_n$ and $I_n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly in
$z\in\mathbb C$. If $K\ge0$ and
$q=|z|^2/[4(K+2)(K+n+2)]<1$, then the tail after terms $k=0,\ldots,K$ has
absolute value at most $|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$, where $a_k$ is the corresponding
series term. The first two differentiated series also converge locally
uniformly.

For $z\ne0$, the functions in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]] satisfy

$$z^2J_n''+zJ_n'+(z^2-n^2)J_n=0, \qquad z^2I_n''+zI_n'-(z^2+n^2)I_n=0.$$

For real or complex $z\ne0$ and integer $n\ge1$, they also satisfy

$$J_{n-1}(z)+J_{n+1}(z)=\frac{2n}{z}J_n(z), \qquad I_{n-1}(z)-I_{n+1}(z)=\frac{2n}{z}I_n(z).$$

In addition, $J_0'(z)=-J_1(z)$.

At $z=0$, the series limits are $J_0(0)=I_0(0)=1$ and
$J_n(0)=I_n(0)=0$ for $n\ge1$.

Fix real $x>0$. Let $D_0(x)=-J_1(x)$ and $D_1(x)=J_0(x)$, and for every integer
$j\ge1$ define

$$D_{j+1}(x)=\frac{2j}{x}D_j(x)-D_{j-1}(x).$$

Thus $D$ is the second sequence obtained from the same order recurrence as
$J_j(x)$. It is a local auxiliary solution, not the Bessel function of the
second kind.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

derivations.claim: Let $h(t)=t-\sin t$. By [F2], $h(0)=0$ and $h'(t)=1-\cos t\ge0$ for $t\ge0$ by [F3], so $\sin t\le t$. Again by [F2] and [F4], $$1-\cos\theta=\int_0^\theta\sin t\,dt \le\int_0^\theta t\,dt=\theta^2/2 \qquad(0\le\theta\le1).$$

For $x\ge1$ and $0\le\theta\le1/\sqrt{x}$, step 1.1 gives $x\cos\theta\ge x-1/2$. Restricting the integral in [F1] to this interval therefore yields $$I_0(x)\ge\frac{e^{x-1/2}}{\pi\sqrt{x}}.$$ The exponential series gives $e^x\ge x^2/2$ for $x\ge0$, so this lower bound is at least $e^{-1/2}x^{3/2}/(2\pi)$ and tends to infinity.

The scaled range in [F1] holds for every $x\ge0$, while step 2.1 shows the unscaled value exceeds any fixed finite range for sufficiently large $x$. The scaled integral method of [[lem-scaled-modified-bessel-midpoint-error]] evaluates the bounded scaled quantity directly.
